Contents may support an ownership check.

content.heading: Check the practical follow-up
content.text: At the end, the staff member explains the next action. Label who will call whom and what the caller should have ready. Practice a thirty-second description of an imaginary lost object using three identifying details, then ask what you should do next. Keep private contact details out of a public practice message.

questions.prompt: What is on the caller’s backpack?
questions.explanation: The caller identifies a yellow star badge on the front.

questions.prompt: Where did the caller last see the backpack?
options: Under a seat on the number twelve bus.
questions.explanation: The caller last saw it under a seat on the number twelve bus.

questions.prompt: Why is the black bag not the caller’s?
options: The caller did not lose any bag.
The black bag is empty and every bag must be empty.
The caller only owns a suitcase.
The caller’s bag is blue and has a star badge.
questions.explanation: The caller rejects the black bag because the missing backpack is blue with a yellow star badge.

lessons.listeningText: Caller: Hello. I left my backpack on the number twelve bus this morning. Staff: Can you describe it? Caller: It is blue, with a yellow star badge on the front. Inside there is a green notebook and a lunch box. I last saw it under my seat near the back. Staff: We have a black bag here. Caller: That is not mine. Staff: The driver is still checking the bus. Please call us again after three. Have your ticket ready so we can check the journey details. Caller: Thank you. I will call after three this afternoon.

lessons.title: Listen: a library on wheels
lessons.description: Understand the main idea and practical details in a short local report.

content.heading: Start with the main purpose
content.text: A short report may begin with a new service and then explain how it works. Listen first for what the service does and who it helps. The title gives you a useful prediction, but the recording supplies the facts. Do not treat every named place as the service’s destination.
examples: A mobile library takes books to people.
Keep the main idea separate from small details.

content.heading: Catch the schedule and borrowing rule
content.text: Write three headings before replaying: visits, borrowing, and registration. The report includes different numbers for different purposes. Match a number to its label before answering a question. A visit frequency is not the same thing as the length of time a person can keep a book.
examples: Frequency: how often the van comes.
Loan period: how long a book may be kept.
Limit: how many books may be borrowed.

content.heading: Retell the report for a neighbour
content.text: Imagine explaining the service to someone who missed the report. Give the purpose, visit day, and one useful rule. Check the registration requirement separately. A brief summary should preserve the key facts without copying every sentence. Leave out details you did not hear rather than filling them with assumptions.
examples: The van visits on a regular day.
Explain how a new member registers.

questions.prompt: Why was the mobile library introduced?
options: Some residents cannot easily reach the town library.
questions.explanation: The report says it helps residents who find travel to the town library difficult.

questions.prompt: How often does the van visit each village?
questions.explanation: The stated schedule is every second Wednesday.

questions.prompt: How many books may each member borrow at a time?
questions.explanation: Members may borrow up to four books at a time.

lessons.listeningText: A new mobile library began visiting local villages this month. The small van carries novels, children’s stories, and books about gardening. The council introduced it because some residents cannot easily travel to the town library. The van visits each village every second Wednesday and stops near the community hall from two until four. Members can borrow up to four books and keep them until the next visit. Joining is free. New members should bring proof of their address when they register. The driver also accepts book returns, but the van does not provide a printing service at present.

lessons.title: Listen: confirm a cottage booking
lessons.description: Track a revised duration, included services, and a check-in arrangement.

content.heading: Expect a final booking summary
content.text: Accommodation calls often contain old information, a change, and a final summary. Listen for the booking name and broad request first. The guest may correct the length of the stay, so avoid writing the first number as your final answer before the call has finished.
examples: A summary confirms the final arrangement.
Listen for what is included in the price.

content.heading: Distinguish an included item from an extra
content.text: Included means covered by the stated price. An optional extra costs more or requires another arrangement. In this call, the guest asks about several useful services. Put them in separate columns after listening. Do not assume that every facility mentioned is automatically part of the booking.
examples: Extra: an additional charge is named.
An available service is not always included.

content.heading: Check arrival instructions in detail
content.text: The call finishes with a plan for arriving after the reception desk closes. Note what the guest will receive and how they will enter. Practice confirming a booking in three sentences: dates or nights, important inclusions, and arrival plan. Keep your summary consistent with the final agreement.

questions.prompt: How many nights is the final booking for?
questions.explanation: The guest changes the original two-night booking to three nights.

questions.prompt: What is included in the cottage price?
questions.explanation: Parking is included; breakfast costs extra.

questions.prompt: How will the guest get the key after reception closes?
options: From a key box using a code sent by text.
By waiting until the next morning.
From a café that is never mentioned.
questions.explanation: The host will text a code for the key box beside the door.

lessons.listeningText: Host: Hello, Willow Cottages. Guest: I have a booking under Patel for two nights from Friday. Could I stay until Monday instead? Host: Yes, I can change it to three nights. Guest: Thank you. Is breakfast included? Host: No, breakfast is eight pounds extra per person, but parking is included. Guest: We will cook our own breakfast. Our train arrives late, so we may reach you at nine. Host: Reception closes at eight. I will text you a code for the key box beside the door. Guest: Perfect. Please confirm the three nights by email as well. Host: Certainly.

lessons.title: Write an opinion with a reason and example
lessons.description: Build one focused paragraph about a familiar choice.

content.heading: State one clear opinion
content.text: An opinion paragraph tells the reader what you think about a focused topic. Choose a familiar question, such as whether studying in the morning suits you. Start with your answer rather than an unrelated history of the topic. Use I think when it helps make the personal viewpoint clear.
examples: I prefer studying in the morning.
For me, a quiet library is a good place to learn.
I think walking is the best way to explore my town.

content.heading: Support the idea with a concrete example
content.text: A reason explains why you hold the opinion. An example shows the reason in a particular situation. Because can connect the opinion and reason; for example introduces a detail. Do not simply repeat the same statement with different adjectives, because the reader still needs supporting information.
examples: I study early because I feel more alert.
For example, I can read a short article before work.
Later in the day, I am often tired.

content.heading: End with a connected final sentence
content.text: Write seventy to ninety words with an opinion, a reason, a concrete example, and a final sentence. Keep all the sentences connected to the same main idea. Read the paragraph and underline the reason and example. If you cannot find them, add a detail that helps the reader understand your choice.
examples: That is why mornings work well for me.
Different learners may prefer a different time.
My choice fits my daily routine.

questions.prompt: Which sentence gives a clear personal opinion?
options: I prefer studying in the morning.
questions.explanation: Prefer directly states the writer’s choice.

questions.prompt: Which detail best supports preferring morning study?
options: I feel alert then and finish reading before work.
questions.explanation: The detail explains why morning study fits the writer’s energy and schedule.

questions.prompt: What should an example do in this paragraph?
options: Show the reason in a specific situation.
Repeat the title without adding detail.
questions.explanation: A specific example helps the reader see how the reason works in practice.

lessons.title: Write a useful place review
lessons.description: Describe an experience, give evidence, and recommend fairly.

content.heading: Give the reader a clear context
content.text: A review helps another person decide whether a place may suit them. Name the kind of place and say when you visited. Choose details a reader can use, such as service, noise, access, or value. Do not present one visit as proof that every visit will be identical.
examples: I visited the Garden Café on Saturday afternoon.
It was busy, but we found a table outside.
We ordered two sandwiches and tea.

content.heading: Support praise and criticism with details
content.text: An adjective such as excellent or terrible is more useful with an example. Explain what happened instead of attacking the people who work there. A balanced review can mention a strength and a limitation, but it should not invent a problem just to sound balanced.
examples: The server brought water without being asked.
Our food took twenty minutes to arrive.
The outdoor tables were beside a noisy road.

content.heading: Make a recommendation for a particular reader
content.text: Finish by explaining whom the place may suit and why. Write eighty to one hundred words with two specific details from an imaginary or real visit. Check past tenses for your visit and present forms for cautiously stated general features. Remove personal information about staff or other customers.
examples: I would recommend it for a quick lunch.
Choose an indoor table if you want a quieter conversation.
I would visit again on a less busy day.

questions.prompt: Which detail gives useful evidence about service?
options: The server brought water without being asked.
questions.explanation: The specific action helps a reader understand what the service was like.

questions.prompt: Which ending gives a useful targeted recommendation?
options: Everyone must love it for every reason.
Choose an indoor table if you want a quieter conversation.
No one can ever disagree with me.
questions.explanation: The recommendation names a reader’s need and a practical choice.

questions.prompt: Which statement fairly limits a review to the writer’s experience?
options: The food is always late for everyone forever.
All workers everywhere are the same.
Nobody has ever enjoyed this place.
The food took twenty minutes during my Saturday visit.
questions.explanation: The selected statement reports a specific observation without an unsupported universal claim.

lessons.title: Write a polite email about a problem
lessons.description: Explain what happened and request a specific solution.

content.heading: Identify the item and the problem
content.text: A helpful problem email names the item or service, gives a date or reference when relevant, and explains the issue. Keep the opening calm and specific. The reader needs enough information to identify the case before deciding what action is possible. Use imaginary details for this practice.
examples: I ordered two notebooks on 8 June.
Only one notebook arrived in the package.

content.heading: State the facts in a clear order
content.text: Explain what you expected and what actually happened. Add a relevant detail, such as the package appearing undamaged, only if it is true in your scenario. Avoid guessing who caused the problem. The past simple describes completed events; the present simple can describe the current situation.
examples: It contained one notebook instead of two.
I still need the second notebook for my class.

content.heading: Ask for one practical next step
content.text: Say what solution you would like and invite a reply. A polite, specific request is easier to act on than an angry general complaint. Write eighty to one hundred words with a subject, greeting, facts, request, and closing. Check the reference number and make sure the request matches the problem.
examples: Could you send the missing notebook, please?
Please let me know when it can be sent.
Thank you for your help. Kind regards, Nila

questions.prompt: Which subject line best identifies the problem?
questions.explanation: The line names both the issue and an identifying order reference.

questions.prompt: Which sentence states a fact without guessing blame?
options: Everyone at the company is careless.
The package contained one notebook instead of two.
questions.explanation: The selected sentence describes the observable problem and avoids unsupported blame.

questions.prompt: Which request directly matches a missing notebook?
options: Could you send the missing notebook, please?
Could you change my neighbour’s job?
questions.explanation: The requested action resolves the specific item that was not delivered.

lessons.title: Say regular past endings clearly
lessons.description: Practice the three common pronunciations of ed in regular past verbs.

content.heading: Listen to the final sound of the base verb
content.text: The spelling ed has three common pronunciations in regular past verbs. After many voiceless sounds, it sounds like t, as in walked. After many voiced sounds, it sounds like d, as in played. The base verb’s final sound matters more than its final written letter.

content.heading: Add a syllable after t or d
content.text: After a base verb ending in a t or d sound, ed adds an extra syllable, often sounding like id. Wanted and needed each have an extra beat compared with want and need. Do not add that extra beat to every regular past verb; played normally stays one syllable.

content.heading: Keep the ending in a short story
content.text: Choose three past actions from yesterday or an imaginary day, with one example of each ending type. Say the sentences slowly and keep the final sounds audible. Then join them with natural pauses. Ask a partner to identify whether you are talking about yesterday or a regular daily habit.

questions.prompt: Which verb normally has an extra syllable in its ed ending?
questions.explanation: Want ends in a t sound, so wanted adds an extra syllable.

questions.prompt: What mainly determines the pronunciation of a regular ed ending?
options: The number of letters in the subject.
The first letter of the sentence.
The final sound of the base verb.
questions.explanation: The base verb’s final sound determines which common ed pronunciation follows.

questions.prompt: Which word normally ends in a t sound?
questions.explanation: Walked has a voiceless final consonant before ed, so the ending is pronounced t.

lessons.title: Make a plan together
lessons.description: Offer a suggestion, respond politely, and settle on a practical arrangement.

content.heading: Offer an activity with a clear phrase
content.text: Use Let’s plus a base verb to suggest a shared action. Shall we plus a base verb is another common suggestion. Add enough information for your partner to react, such as the activity and a possible time. Speak with a friendly tone rather than treating a suggestion as an order.
examples: Shall we meet at the library?
How about going for a walk?

content.heading: Accept or suggest an alternative
content.text: A positive response can be short, but add a useful detail to move the plan forward. If the suggestion does not suit you, give a brief reason and offer an alternative. You do not need a long apology. The goal is an arrangement that works for both people.
examples: I can’t on Friday. How about Saturday?
I prefer the café because it is nearer.

content.heading: Confirm the final plan clearly
content.text: Once you agree, summarize the activity, place, and time. Stress the important words gently so the listener notices them. Ask a short confirmation question if any detail is uncertain. Practice a one-minute exchange in which the first suggestion changes before you agree on a final plan.
examples: So, Saturday at ten in the library.
Is that the library near the park?

questions.prompt: Which phrase makes a shared suggestion correctly?
questions.explanation: Let’s takes the base verb meet.

questions.prompt: Which response politely offers an alternative?
options: I can’t on Friday. How about Saturday?
No, and I refuse to explain anything.
questions.explanation: The response gives a brief limit and another possible day.

questions.prompt: Which details should a final plan usually confirm?
options: Only the colour of a pen.
An unrelated weather event from last year.
questions.explanation: Those practical details let both people act on the agreement.

lessons.title: Explain again when a word is missing
lessons.description: Use descriptions, clarification, and polite repair to keep speaking.

content.heading: Describe a word you cannot remember
content.text: If you forget a word, explain its purpose, appearance, or category. Use simple language you already know instead of stopping completely. The listener may help with the word. A clear description can communicate successfully even when it is longer than the exact word you wanted.
examples: It is the thing you use to open a bottle.
It is a place where you borrow books.
It is round and you kick it in a game.

content.heading: Check the part you did not understand
content.text: Ask a focused question rather than repeating I don’t understand for the whole conversation. You can ask what a word means or check one detail. Repeat the interpretation you think is right and let the speaker confirm or correct it. This gives both people a way forward.
examples: Do you mean the station entrance?
Did you say fifteen or fifty?

content.heading: Correct yourself in a short, calm way
content.text: A repair is a small correction during speaking. Use sorry, I mean to replace an incorrect detail without restarting the entire conversation. Practice describing an object, clarifying one number, and correcting one date. Pause between ideas so your listener has enough time to follow the new information.
examples: We meet on Monday—sorry, I mean Tuesday.
Let me say that another way.

questions.prompt: You forget the word library. Which description helps?
options: A place where you borrow books.
A thing you wear on your feet.
questions.explanation: The description gives the defining everyday purpose of a library.

questions.prompt: Which phrase politely corrects your own mistake?
questions.explanation: I mean introduces the corrected detail without restarting the whole message.

questions.prompt: Which question checks an unclear number?
options: Did you say fifteen or fifty?
questions.explanation: The question isolates the number contrast that needs clarification.

words.meaning: An opening with glass that lets light into a room.
words.example: Please open the window.

words.meaning: A small object used to open a lock.
words.example: My key is in my bag.

words.meaning: A piece of furniture with a flat top.
words.example: The book is on the table.

words.meaning: Something you wear on a foot.
words.example: This shoe is black.

words.meaning: A piece of clothing for the upper part of the body.
words.example: I have a blue shirt.

words.meaning: The colour of a ripe tomato.
words.example: Her bag is red.

words.meaning: The body part at the end of your arm.
words.example: This is my left hand.

words.meaning: The plural of foot; the body parts you stand on.
words.example: My feet are cold.

words.meaning: Wanting or needing food.
words.example: I am hungry after class.

words.meaning: Wanting or needing a drink.
words.example: He is thirsty and wants water.

words.meaning: The day after Sunday and before Tuesday.
words.example: Our class is on Monday.

words.meaning: The day that is happening now.
words.example: Today is Friday.

words.meaning: In a position below something.
words.example: The bag is under the chair.

words.meaning: A short distance away.
words.example: My home is near the school.

words.meaning: A word used to make a request polite.
words.example: A pen, please.

words.meaning: Prepared to do something.
words.example: We are ready for class.

words.meaning: To remove the outer skin of a fruit or vegetable.
words.example: Peel the banana before eating it.

words.meaning: To make a liquid flow into or out of a container.
words.example: Pour the water into a glass.

words.meaning: To move a spoon or similar tool around in a liquid or mixture.
words.example: Stir the soup with a spoon.

words.meaning: Having many clouds in the sky.
words.example: It is cloudy this morning.

words.meaning: An object held above you to protect you from rain.
words.example: Bring an umbrella because rain is expected.

words.meaning: One of the periods into which a year is divided by weather or daylight patterns.
words.example: This is the wet season here.

words.meaning: A person whose work is repairing machines or vehicles.
words.example: A mechanic repaired our car.

words.meaning: A place where bread and similar foods are made or sold.
words.example: I buy fresh bread at the bakery.

words.meaning: A person receiving care from a medical professional.
words.example: The nurse spoke to the patient.

words.meaning: A person who welcomes visitors and helps organize appointments.
words.example: The receptionist confirmed my haircut time.

words.meaning: To put your name on an official list for an activity or service.
words.example: Please register before your first class.

words.meaning: To give one thing and receive another in return.
words.example: We exchange books at the club.

words.meaning: In place of another person, thing, or action.
words.example: I cannot come on Friday; let us meet on Saturday instead.

words.meaning: In total, after everything is included.
words.example: The fruit costs three pounds altogether.

words.meaning: Without waiting; at once.
words.example: Serve the snack immediately.

words.meaning: After everything else; at the last step.
words.example: Finally, press Save.

words.meaning: A physical or mental change that may indicate a health condition.
words.example: A cough can be a symptom of several different conditions.

words.meaning: An authorized instruction for supplying a medicine.
words.example: The pharmacist checked the prescription.

words.meaning: Feeling better because a worry or difficulty has ended.
